analysis.title: US Economic Weekly - The consumer has moved past the Fed's 2025 snapshot
key_insights: The 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) shows real median family income up 7% since the 2022 survey, to $82,200. Real mean income fell 6% (down 1% excluding the top 1%), mainly from the 2021 ARPA transfer surge and the inflation wave. Gains were uneven across the income and wealth distributions.

Wage growth turned K-shaped in late 2024, with higher-income wages outpacing lower-income wages. The gap reversed in July 2026 in BofA internal data. In September, after-tax wage growth was 4.5% y/y for lower-income households versus 3.8% for middle- and higher-income households. Lower withholding after the OBBBA and broader hiring both contributed.

Spending growth was also K-shaped from late 2024, led by higher-income households backed by equity wealth. Since the summer the spending K has narrowed, with lower-income card spending strengthening. BofA says this makes its bullish consumer outlook more sustainable.

Real median net worth rose 2% and real mean net worth rose 7% between the 2022 and 2025 SCF. Most SCF interviews fall in 2Q 2025, after the Liberation Day equity selloff and before the later rally. Flow of Funds real net worth per household rose about 6% from 2Q 2022 to 2Q 2025 and another 6% from 2Q 2025 to 2Q 2026. Gains remain concentrated among higher-income households.

Housing: the homeownership rate declined from the 2022 to the 2025 survey and the median home costs more than 4.5 times median family income. BofA does not expect affordability to have improved this year given high borrowing costs and the Fed's September rate hike. Stock market participation edged down from 58% to 56%, above the 2019 level of 53%.

Debt looks manageable against assets: the leverage ratio fell to 10% and 77% of families hold debt. Against income it looks worse. The payment-to-income ratio rose 2pp to 11.9%, and debt-to-income rose from 89.4% to 94.9%. The share of families spending more than 40% of income on debt payments rose from 8.4% to 11.1%, the highest since 2013.

September CPI and PPI both surprised to the upside, with core goods and core services both accelerating. AI and Iran continued to push inflation up, and the rebound in rent and OER suggests housing disinflation may have run its course. BofA projects September headline PCE at 0.52% m/m (3.1% y/y) and core PCE at 0.34% m/m (3.7% y/y).

September retail sales were mixed. The control group rose 0.1% against 0.3% consensus, while food services rose 1.1%. Prior two months were revised up. Real spending is tracking +3.5% q/q saar for 3Q.
3Q GDP tracking rose one tenth to 3.6% q/q saar on stronger food services and August business inventories. BofA's official 3Q GDP forecast is 3.5%.

BofA keeps its out-of-consensus call for 25bp Fed hikes in October and December. The Fed hiked 25bp in September under Chair Warsh with a hawkish message. Recent Fed speak suggests the committee may lean toward a quarterly cadence. The FOMC minutes said most participants saw another hike as likely appropriate by year end.

Fed speakers are split on pace. Logan sees 50bp or more needed, Waller floated 25bp every other meeting up to 75bp total, Collins and Williams see one more hike, and Bowman sees no urgency. The Fed is in blackout from Oct 17 ahead of the Oct 27-28 meeting.

Core views: BofA forecasts 2026 GDP growth of 2.6% 4Q/4Q and 2.1% for 2027, and core PCE finishing 2026 slightly above 3%. It expects 2.5% core PCE in 2027 and job growth averaging 70k a month in 2026, with the unemployment rate at 4.1% through 2027. BofA says risks to its inflation forecast skew to the upside.

BofA's rates forecast has 10-year Treasury yields at 5.00% by December 2026 (spot 5.09%), the 2-year at 5.00% (spot 4.75%), and USD-JPY at 149 (spot 157.89). It sees EUR-USD at 1.15 by December 2026 (spot 1.12).

Next week's calendar is light and housing-focused: NAHB (Mon), housing starts and pending home sales (Tue), jobless claims (Thu), and preliminary October S&P Global PMIs and UMich sentiment (Fri). BofA's services PMI estimate is 59.7 versus 57.7 consensus, and its pending home sales estimate is 1.9% versus 0.5% consensus.

sector_views.rationale: Affordability is near historical lows, with the median home above 4.5 times median income. Mortgage rates are elevated and the Fed resumed hiking. Residential investment is forecast to decline in 2026 (-3.0%).

tension_points.bull_case: Lower-income wage growth (4.5% y/y) now exceeds higher-income (3.8%), the spending K is narrowing, hiring has strengthened and layoffs are low. This supports a sustainable consumer outlook and real spending tracking +3.5% q/q saar.
tension_points.bear_case: Wealth gains remain concentrated at the top and the share of families with debt payments above 40% of income rose to 11.1%. Debt-to-income is up and housing affordability is stretched.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Lower-income wage and spending growth falling back below higher-income growth, or the equity rally reversing and removing the wealth effect that supports top-income spending.
